headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
headings.content: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is an essential emergency life-saving procedure performed when an individual's heart stops beating or they stop breathing effectively. The primary goal of CPR is to manually maintain a state of systemic circulation and oxygenation to vital organs, particularly the brain and the heart, until advanced medical help arrives or spontaneous circulation is restored. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding the core physiological principles of CPR is critical, as you will encounter cardiac arrest situations in various clinical and community settings. Cardiac arrest leads to a sudden cessation of blood flow, causing cellular hypoxia and irreversible tissue damage within minutes if intervention is delayed. CPR combines chest compressions to artificially pump blood and artificial ventilation to deliver oxygen into the lungs. Effective CPR relies on minimizing interruptions in chest compressions and ensuring adequate depth and rate. The Nigerian healthcare environment often demands resource-improvisation and rapid clinical judgment, making foundational BLS skills mandatory for all nursing professionals. By mastering the principles of CPR, you bridge the gap between sudden clinical deterioration and advanced lifesaving interventions, drastically improving patient morbidity and mortality outcomes.

headings.title: The Chain of Survival in Basic Life Support
headings.content: The Chain of Survival in Basic Life Support (BLS) provides a structured, sequential framework of care that maximizes the chances of survival for an individual experiencing cardiac arrest. For adult victims, the standard chain comprises several interconnected links: immediate recognition of cardiac arrest and prevention, early activation of the emergency response system (such as calling local emergency numbers in Nigeria), early CPR emphasizing chest compressions, rapid defibrillation with an Automated External Defibrillator (AED), and integrated post-cardiac arrest care. Each link is dependent on the success of the preceding one; a breakdown anywhere along the chain significantly decreases survival rates. In resource-limited or busy clinical environments, nurses must be adept at quickly identifying arrest cues and orchestrating the activation of emergency teams without delay. Early bystander intervention through high-quality chest compressions buys critical time before defibrillation can be achieved. Furthermore, post-resuscitation care focuses on stabilizing the patient, optimizing ventilation and perfusion, and identifying the precipitating cause of the cardiac event. Understanding this chain empowers nursing students to act methodically, prioritize interventions, and educate communities on the importance of early recognition and rapid response.

headings.title: Assessment of the Scene and Patient Responsiveness
headings.content: Assessing the scene and patient responsiveness is the mandatory first step before initiating any rescue attempt. As a nursing student, your safety is paramount; you must first ensure that the environment is free from hazards such as live electrical wires, heavy traffic, or structural dangers before approaching the victim. Once safety is established, you approach the patient and assess responsiveness by tapping their shoulders firmly and shouting loudly, 'Are you okay?' At the same time, quickly observe the patient's chest for any normal or abnormal breathing patterns (such as gasping, known as agonal respirations, which do not count as normal breathing). This assessment should take no longer than 10 seconds to avoid wasting precious time. If the patient does not respond and is either not breathing or only gasping, you must immediately activate the emergency response system and retrieve an AED if available. In a hospital or clinical ward setting, this involves calling for assistance, alerting the code team, and bringing emergency equipment to the bedside. Thorough assessment prevents unnecessary interventions on responsive patients while ensuring that true cardiac arrest victims receive rapid, uncompromised care.

headings.title: Airway Management and Breathing Assessment
headings.content: Managing the airway and assessing breathing are critical components of basic life support that follow responsiveness checks. If cardiac arrest is suspected, the airway must be opened to allow for potential airflow and subsequent rescue ventilations. For a patient without suspected trauma, the preferred maneuver is the head-tilt/chin-lift technique, which lifts the tongue away from the back of the pharynx and clears the upper airway. If a cervical spine injury is suspected—such as in a motor vehicle accident common on Nigerian roads—the jaw-thrust maneuver is utilized to minimize neck movement while opening the airway. While maintaining the open airway, the nurse looks for chest rise, listens for airflow, and feels for breath against their cheek for no more than 10 seconds. If the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally, rescue breaths can be delivered using barrier devices like pocket masks or bag-valve-mask (BVM) devices if trained personnel and equipment are present. Each breath should be delivered over about one second, making the chest visibly rise. However, in standard bystander or single-rescuer adult BLS where immediate ventilatory equipment is lacking, continuous high-quality chest compressions are prioritized over rescue breaths in the first few minutes, though combined compression-ventilation ratios (30:2) remain the standard when performing full CPR.

headings.title: Performing High-Quality Chest Compressions
headings.content: Performing high-quality chest compressions is the most crucial element of effective CPR, directly determining the patient's chance of survival. High-quality compressions generate critical blood flow to the heart and brain. To perform this correctly, the patient must be placed on a firm, flat surface. The rescuer kneels beside the patient, places the heel of one hand on the center of the patient's chest (lower half of the breastbone/sternum) and puts the other hand on top, interlocking the fingers. Keep your arms completely straight, position your shoulders directly over your hands, and use your upper body weight to push straight down. For an adult, compress the chest to a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not greater than 2.4 inches (6 cm). Maintain a compression rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Crucially, allow full chest recoil after each compression to let the heart refill with blood before the next stroke. Minimize any interruptions in chest compressions, keeping pauses to less than 10 seconds, even when delivering breaths or checking rhythms. For Nigerian nursing students, practicing these parameters on simulation mannequins builds the muscle memory required to sustain effective compressions during high-stress clinical emergencies.

headings.title: Use of the Automated External Defibrillator (AED)
headings.content: The Automated External Defibrillator (AED) is a computerized medical device that can analyze a patient's cardiac rhythm, identify shockable rhythms such as ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT), and deliver an electrical shock to restore a normal heart rhythm. AEDs are increasingly deployed in public spaces and clinical wards across Nigeria. When an AED arrives, turn it on immediately and follow its visual and voice prompts. First, bare the patient's chest, wiping it dry if necessary, and apply the adhesive electrode pads according to the diagrams on the pads (typically right upper chest and left lower lateral chest). If the patient has excessive chest hair, a quick shave might be needed to ensure proper pad adhesion, and medication patches should be removed and wiped clean. Once the pads are attached, the AED will prompt you to clear the patient so it can analyze the rhythm. Ensure that no one is touching the patient during analysis and shock delivery. If a shock is advised, the machine will charge and instruct you to press the shock button. Immediately resume high-quality chest compressions starting with compressions after the shock is delivered, following the CPR-to-AED cycle until advanced medical personnel take over.

headings.title: Special Considerations in CPR and Complications
headings.content: Performing CPR can present various special clinical considerations and potential complications that nurses must anticipate and manage. Common physical complications arising from chest compressions include rib fractures, sternal fractures, costochondral separation, and pneumothorax, especially in elderly patients with decreased bone density. Despite these risks, life preservation takes precedence, and compressions must continue without hesitation. Other considerations involve foreign body airway obstructions, pregnant patients, and pediatric populations, where anatomical differences require modified techniques (such as using two fingers for infants or different compression-to-ventilation ratios). In pregnant patients, aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus can severely compromise venous return; thus, manual left uterine displacement or tilting the backboard can improve resuscitation efficacy. Additionally, gastric inflation often occurs during rescue breathing, increasing the risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Nurses should position the airway correctly and avoid excessive ventilation volumes or forceful breath delivery to minimize this risk. Recognizing and preparing for these nuances ensures safe, comprehensive, and patient-tailored resuscitation efforts in diverse clinical scenarios.

headings.title: Termination of Resuscitation and Nursing Documentation
headings.content: The termination of resuscitation and accurate nursing documentation are final, vital responsibilities in any cardiac arrest event. Resuscitation efforts are generally continued until the patient achieves Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC), trained advanced life support (ALS) personnel arrive and take over, signs of irreversible death (such as rigor mortis or decapitation) appear, or a valid Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order is presented. In many clinical settings, a physician makes the formal decision to cease resuscitation based on downtime, patient comorbidities, and lack of response to prolonged advanced interventions. Once CPR ends, meticulous nursing documentation is legally and professionally mandatory. The nursing record must detail the exact time the collapse was noted or suspected, the time CPR was initiated, the sequence of interventions (including compression quality and interruptions), AED analyses and shock deliveries administered, administration of any emergency drugs, the patient's response, and the exact time resuscitation was terminated or ROSC was achieved. Clear documentation protects healthcare professionals legally, ensures continuity of care, and provides essential data for clinical audits and quality improvement in Nigerian healthcare facilities.
